problem: The last sentence gives the book's own verdict ('since the data came first') on a contested credit question. It should be framed as a position.

fix.digest: Nature printed the Watson–Crick structure, then 'Molecular Structure of Deoxypentose Nucleic Acids' by Wilkins, Stokes and Herbert Wilson, then Franklin and Gosling's 'Molecular Configuration in Sodium Thymonucleate'. The King's papers presented the diffraction theory and data that supported a helix; Franklin and Gosling's printed Photograph 51 as its only figure. Read in order, the issue looked like experimental confirmation of a Cambridge idea. Critics have questioned that framing, pointing out that the King's data had come first.

problem: 'The two groups reached overlapping conclusions independently' is a verdict on the most contested point, since Crick's C2 reading used Franklin's own measurements from the MRC report. It should be presented as a position.

fix.note: In the same fortnight Crick read two antiparallel chains in Franklin's C2 data from the report Perutz had passed on, and Franklin wrote that both forms were two-chain helices. Days later Watson found the base pairs. Franklin reached her conclusions by her own analysis; the Cambridge pair reached theirs by model-building that drew on her measurements in the MRC report. How independent the two routes were is part of the credit debate.

problem: 'Lawfully passed' is a loaded word that Wilkins's account does not use. His account is that the pattern was properly in his hands.

fix.note: The most disputed day in the record. Watson's memoir makes it a revelation, and Wilkins describes a pattern properly passed to him. Gosling later said it was Franklin's own handover gift, while other histories say she did not know. Her notebook, meanwhile, shows her own analysis already pointing to two chains.

problem: 'The order of the papers... shaped how credit was seen' is stated as the book's own verdict. It should be attributed.

fix.note: The papers were printed one after another, with the model first and the data after. Pauling had just written that the King's data explained why Cambridge had won. Historians have argued that the order of the papers, more than any single sentence in them, shaped how credit was seen.
